LUNAR 30 Mission Control is an interactive lunar survival simulator developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Designed for young learners, it places players in command of Artemis Outpost Shackleton, where they must lead a four-member astronaut crew through a seven-day lunar mission.

Players make critical decisions involving oxygen, water, food, power, radiation protection, equipment failures, and scientific exploration. Each decision has consequences for crew safety, available resources, and mission success. Players can also complete scientific objectives, unlock discoveries, and review their performance through a final after-action report.

The project combines real NASA scientific observations and engineering reference values with simulated mission scenarios. It also integrates NASA's DONKI API to retrieve recent solar flare and solar energetic particle data when available.

LUNAR 30 makes the complexities of lunar exploration accessible and engaging, helping young learners understand the engineering trade-offs, resource management, and decision-making required to sustain human life beyond Earth.
details:
Project Details — LUNAR 30: Mission Control

LUNAR 30 is an interactive, browser-based lunar survival simulator that places players in command of Artemis Outpost Shackleton, a fictional lunar research base. The objective is to keep a four-member astronaut crew alive and operational throughout a seven-day mission while managing limited resources and responding to unexpected challenges.

How It Works

Players monitor five essential resources: oxygen, water, food, electrical power, and radiation protection. Each mission day introduces a scenario, such as equipment failure, solar activity, medical emergencies, or scientific exploration. Players must evaluate the available options and make decisions that affect resource levels, crew health, mission objectives, and their final score.

The game features individual astronaut status monitoring, a mission log, a lunar outpost map, scientific discoveries, mission objectives, and a final after-action report. Successful decisions allow players to complete experiments, unlock discoveries, and achieve mission success, while poor resource management can jeopardize the crew and mission.

NASA Science and Data Integration

The project combines educational gameplay with real scientific references, including NASA's Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document (BVAD), Apollo lunar seismic observations, and the LCROSS mission's findings on lunar water ice.

It also integrates NASA's DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information) API to retrieve recent solar flare and solar energetic particle records. When live records are unavailable, clearly labelled simulated scenarios ensure that gameplay remains functional.

Benefits and Intended Impact

LUNAR 30 aims to make lunar exploration and space science accessible to young learners. Instead of simply reading about the challenges of living on the Moon, players experience the trade-offs involved in maintaining life-support systems, protecting astronauts, allocating resources, and conducting scientific research. It encourages critical thinking, decision-making, resource management, and curiosity about human space exploration.

Technology and Development

The project was developed using:

  • HTML5 for the application structure.
  • CSS3 for the visual design and responsive interface.
  • Vanilla JavaScript for gameplay logic, resource management, event systems, scoring, and interactive features.
  • NASA DONKI API for space-weather data retrieval.
  • NASA NTRS and other NASA scientific resources for engineering reference values and scientific information.

The application requires no backend or framework and is designed to run directly in a modern web browser.

Creativity and Design Considerations

Our creative approach was to transform a complex lunar mission into a playable mission-control experience. We designed a seven-day progression with interconnected decisions rather than isolated trivia questions. The interface uses a mission-control aesthetic, live resource indicators, astronaut status panels, and a mission log to create an immersive experience.

During development, we considered scientific accuracy, accessibility, gameplay balance, and the distinction between actual NASA information and fictional gameplay scenarios.
